title: Playing for nothing, 'cutting a ham', and hauling bass on the streetcar
summary: Breaux explains the term for a dance with no customers, tells the Isaiah Morgan story, describes streetcar bass fares and mentions recording a trio session with Fats Pichon.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: What was the bottom price during the Depression?
Let me turn this, uh, real over.
Bottom price? A lot of times nothing. I mean, it's just one of them things, man. You probably want to win.
Okay, it's going again. Okay, sometimes just nothing at all. That's right. I mean, you go play for a dance.

I mean, you, you, the, guy come get you and say we got a dance at you, such a place. Well, you go ahead on. You go there and people, the customers don't show up as they was, uh, expected. You want to call out a ham. Yeah, that's right. You would cut a ham. Take a ham. Uh-huh. I went all over here to Bugalooza and cut a ham with Isaiah Morgan. But that wasn't no ham. It was a mistake on Isaiah part. We was a week ahead of time. That's true. We left here to go to Bugalooza with Isaiah and got over to the place and started packing the instrument. The man came outside and said, where are you all going? So Ike said, we're playing here tonight. He said, tonight. So who you playing for? So Ike told him the man's name. He said, oh, that's me. He said, you know dance tonight? He said, oh, yes, sir. He went in his pocket to get the, the leather, you know? And he read it. He was a week ahead of time. The dance was a foreign set. That was, that was a big fat ham. Well, it was just a misunderstanding on Isaiah's part. And he said, I'm not going. I said, I'm going. I said, we're playing here tonight. I said, tonight. I said, who you playing for? So Ike told him the man's name. He said, oh, that's me. He said, you know dance tonight?
Why did you call it cut a ham? Cut a ham?

Well, I mean, I imagine you could have called it something else, but I mean. He didn't do no business. He just didn't do any business. He cut a ham. He see for yourself. Yeah, the boys would come tell you. He said, well, you see for yourself. There's no customers. You boys think you want a drink?
That's better down there, y'all. Go around, boy.

Take anything you want. And if it be too far, I could, we have to go. We have to go up to Carlton or maybe on the same, but not. He said, well, I'll tell you what to do. He said, I'll give you a little coffee. Well, at that time, taxes wasn't as plentiful as they are now. I mean, you'd go to job bass drumming all on the street car until just before we stopped having so many street cars, you'd have to go to the public service, get a special permit to bring a set of drums or bass violins on the street car because, yeah, I mean, oh, they claim if somebody hurts themselves or something or another. Then sometimes they used to make you pay extra car fare for it. The car fare for you and the car fare for your bass. The same thing with drums. stuff I know Fats very well. I cut a couple of records with Fats. I don't think they sold, though. It was a trio deal. Fats, Pichon, Paul Barber, and myself. Oh, at Cosmo. This is a good while ago. But actually working with Fats, I don't recall ever working with Fats on his engagement or anybody else's. I've been around a lot. You've been working on the boat?
